title: Six Complaints, Five Examinations, One Phone Call Never Made: the SEC’s Own Report on Missing Madoff
participants: Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities LLC
SEC Office of Compliance Inspections and Examinations

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was the fiction of a trade. The scheme required only that statements be produced; the OIG establishes the gap between the paper and the holdings with a single comparison it ran itself — one feeder-fund statement claiming "approximately $2.5 billion of S&P 100 equities as of January 31, 2005" against DTC records showing Madoff held "less than $18 million worth of S&P 100 equities in his DTC account" on that date.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: What was compromised was the examination function, repeatedly and on the record. "Despite three examinations and two investigations being conducted, a thorough and competent investigation or examination was never performed." The information to trigger a real one was not lacking: "the SEC received more than ample information in the form of detailed and substantive complaints over the years", six of them between June 1992 and December 2008, each raising "significant red flags concerning Madoff’s hedge fund operations".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog was not that nobody could see; it was that nobody checked. The OIG names the omission exactly: "This was perhaps the most egregious failure in the Enforcement investigation of Madoff; that they never verified Madoff’s purported trading with any independent third parties." A senior SEC examiner is quoted on why that mattered: someone running a Ponzi "is not going to hesitate to lie or create records", so the "only way to verify" is "independent third-party verification" like DTC.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was continuation. Madoff’s own account, recorded by the OIG, is of a man who believed the scheme was finished and found that it was not: he "thought he was caught after his testimony about the DTC account", and said of the moment he gave the account number, "I thought it was the end game, over. Monday morning they'll call DTC and this will be over . . . and it never happened." He "was astonished" when Enforcement did not follow up.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment here is the one that did not happen, and that is why the dossier exists. The SEC’s own Inspector General investigated the agency and published a public version naming the failures in its own words. It is an internal review with the limits of one: it examines the conduct of a regulator, makes no finding about any investor’s losses, and determines no liability.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A disclosure-and-examination regime in which a registered broker-dealer’s own books are the first and often the only evidence of what it holds.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The post-Madoff examination reforms and the custody-rule tightening that followed — and this report itself, an agency publishing a forensic account of its own failure.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Each examination that closed without independent verification became part of the record that the firm had been examined; the fact of having been examined reassured the next complainant’s audience; and the complaints kept arriving at an agency that had, in its own words, never performed a competent one.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the SEC was bought: that Madoff’s family connection inside the agency — his niece’s relationship with an SEC assistant director — is why five separate encounters with the regulator produced nothing.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The SEC’s own Inspector General investigated precisely that theory and rejected it on the evidence. It "did not find evidence that any SEC personnel who worked on an SEC examination or investigation of" the firm "had any financial or other inappropriate connection with Bernard Madoff or the Madoff family that influenced the conduct of their examination or investigatory work"; it "did not find that former SEC Assistant Director Eric Swanson’s romantic relationship with Bernard Madoff’s niece, Shana Madoff, influenced the conduct of the SEC examinations", finding that the relationship "did not begin until March of 2006, nearly a year after the OCIE examination he had conducted had been completed in June of 2005"; and it found no evidence of senior officials attempting to influence or interfering with the staff’s work. The documented failure is worse than the rumour in one specific way: corruption would at least imply someone understood what they were covering up. What the OIG describes is an agency that had the account number and never rang the custodian.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Six substantive complaints to the SEC between June 1992 and December 2008, each raising significant red flags, plus two articles in reputable publications in 2001 questioning the returns. Three examinations and two investigations, and "a thorough and competent investigation or examination was never performed". No independent third-party verification of the trading at any point, which the OIG calls perhaps the most egregious failure of the Enforcement investigation. A feeder-fund statement claiming about $2.5 billion in S&P 100 equities on 31 January 2005 against DTC records showing under $18 million held that day. And Madoff’s own statement that he expected the DTC call to end it, and was astonished when it never came.

citations.title: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Office of Investigations, Investigation of Failure of the SEC to Uncover Bernard Madoff’s Ponzi Scheme — Report of Investigation, Case No. OIG-509, Public Version, 31 August 2009
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from sec.gov and read as extracted text. (sec.gov returns 403 to a generic browser user-agent; it serves the file to a request that declares an identity and contact address, which is what the agency asks for.) WHAT THE OIG LOOKED FOR AND DID NOT FIND, from the Executive Summary: "The OIG investigation did not find evidence that any SEC personnel who worked on an SEC examination or investigation of Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities, LLC (BMIS) had any financial or other inappropriate connection with Bernard Madoff or the Madoff family that influenced the conduct of their examination or investigatory work. The OIG also did not find that former SEC Assistant Director Eric Swanson’s romantic relationship with Bernard Madoff’s niece, Shana Madoff, influenced the conduct of the SEC examinations of Madoff and his firm. We also did not find that senior officials at the SEC directly attempted to influence examinations or investigations of Madoff or the Madoff firm, nor was there evidence any senior SEC official interfered with the staff’s ability to perform its work." On the relationship specifically, it found the romance "did not begin until March of 2006, nearly a year after the OCIE examination he had conducted had been completed in June of 2005", and "no evidence that Swanson shared information regarding SEC examinations or investigations of Madoff with Shana while Swanson was at the SEC." WHAT IT DID FIND, in the same summary: "The OIG investigation did find, however, that the SEC received more than ample information in the form of detailed and substantive complaints over the years to warrant a thorough and comprehensive examination and/or investigation of Bernard Madoff and BMIS for operating a Ponzi scheme, and that despite three examinations and two investigations being conducted, a thorough and competent investigation or examination was never performed. The OIG found that between June 1992 and December 2008 when Madoff confessed, the SEC received six substantive complaints that raised significant red flags concerning Madoff’s hedge fund operations and should have led to questions about whether Madoff was actually engaged in trading." THE SINGLE MOST DAMNING PASSAGE, on verification: "This was perhaps the most egregious failure in the Enforcement investigation of Madoff; that they never verified Madoff’s purported trading with any independent third parties." The OIG made the check itself: "We reviewed a January 2005 statement for one Madoff feeder fund account, which alone indicated that it held approximately $2.5 billion of S&P 100 equities as of January 31, 2005. On the contrary, on January 31, 2005, DTC records show that Madoff held less than $18 million worth of S&P 100 equities in his DTC account." And Madoff’s own account of the moment: he "stated that he had thought he was caught after his testimony about the DTC account, noting that when they asked for the DTC account number, 'I thought it was the end game, over. Monday morning they'll call DTC and this will be over . . . and it never happened'", and that when Enforcement did not follow up he "was astonished". This is an inspector-general report on the conduct of a regulator. It makes no finding about any investor’s losses and determines no liability.
